questions.q: Why do you pass a seed to np.random.default_rng(42)?
options: To make the random numbers more random
To make the sequence reproducible: the same seed gives the same numbers
To limit the numbers to values below 42
To generate exactly 42 numbers
questions.explain: Computer random numbers come from a formula, and the seed sets the starting point. The same seed produces the same sequence, which makes analyses reproducible.

questions.q: What values can rng.integers(1, 7, size=10) produce?
options: Whole numbers from 1 to 7 inclusive
Whole numbers from 0 to 7
Whole numbers from 1 to 6, because the upper end is excluded
Decimals between 1 and 7
questions.explain: Like range, integers excludes the upper bound, so 1 to 7 gives dice values 1 through 6.

questions.q: What does rng.choice(a, size=3, replace=False) do?
options: Picks three items, and the same item may appear twice
Picks three distinct items from a
Shuffles a in place and returns nothing
Returns the three smallest items of a
questions.explain: replace=False samples without replacement, so no item can be picked more than once. The default, replace=True, allows repeats.

questions.q: In the dice simulation, why does (rolls == 7).mean() give the fraction of rolls that were 7?
options: Because mean always returns a probability
Because rolls == 7 removes every roll that is not 7
Because NumPy converts the array to percentages
Because True counts as 1 and False as 0, so the mean of the boolean array is the share of True values
questions.explain: Averaging a boolean array treats True as 1 and False as 0, giving the proportion of True values.

questions.q: What is a bootstrap in this lesson?
options: Resampling your data with replacement many times to see how a statistic varies
Restarting the generator with a new seed
Sorting an array before sampling
Removing outliers from a sample
questions.explain: The bootstrap draws many samples with replacement from your data and recomputes the statistic each time; the spread of the results shows its uncertainty.
